reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: A rare form of trichobezoar in which a gastric hair mass has a tail extending through the pylorus into the small bowel
Almost always occurs in young females with underlying trichotillomania (hair-pulling) and trichophagia (hair-eating)
Presents with epigastric pain, early satiety, a palpable abdominal mass, weight loss, and sometimes halitosis
Complications include gastric ulceration, obstruction, perforation, and, rarely, intussusception or pancreatitis
A firm, mobile, mouldable epigastric mass on examination is a valuable clue
Cross-sectional imaging or endoscopy demonstrates the intragastric mass with its characteristic small-bowel tail
Definitive management is surgical or endoscopic removal together with psychiatric treatment of the underlying hair-pulling disorder to prevent recurrence
reference.pathophysiology: Rapunzel syndrome arises when compulsively ingested hair (trichophagia), which is indigestible and slippery, becomes trapped in the gastric folds and enmeshes with mucus and food debris to form a trichobezoar. Over time the mass conforms to the shape of the stomach and a long tail extends through the pylorus into the small intestine. The accumulating mass impairs gastric emptying, causes mucosal pressure necrosis and ulceration, and can precipitate obstruction or perforation; the behavioural substrate is an impulse-control/psychiatric disorder driving repeated hair ingestion.
additionalDifferentials: Gastric outlet obstruction from other causes
Gastric or abdominal neoplasm presenting as a mass
additionalInvestigations: Upper endoscopy to visualise and characterise the bezoar
CT of the abdomen to define the mass, its tail, and complications
Upper gastrointestinal contrast study demonstrating a mobile intraluminal filling defect
Full blood count and iron studies to assess anaemia and nutritional status
Psychiatric assessment for trichotillomania and trichophagia
redFlags: Signs of gastrointestinal perforation or peritonitis
Complete gastric outlet or small-bowel obstruction
Significant gastrointestinal bleeding from mucosal ulceration
reference.prognosis: With complete removal of the bezoar and effective treatment of the underlying psychiatric disorder the prognosis is good, but failure to address the hair-pulling behaviour commonly leads to recurrence.
pitfalls: Removing the bezoar without treating the underlying trichotillomania, inviting recurrence
Underestimating the extent of the small-bowel tail before intervention
Missing complications such as ulceration, obstruction, or perforation
Failing to consider the diagnosis in a young woman with an epigastric mass and weight loss
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Surgical removal of the trichobezoar, usually by laparotomy given the size and small-bowel tail, with endoscopic removal reserved for small masses
Management of complications such as gastric ulceration, obstruction or perforation at the time of intervention
Correction of anaemia and nutritional deficiency with iron and dietary support
Psychiatric treatment of the underlying trichotillomania and trichophagia with habit-reversal behavioural therapy and consideration of an SSRI
Long-term psychiatric and family follow-up to detect and prevent recurrence, which is common if the behaviour is not addressed
Combined surgical and psychiatric multidisciplinary management
